chunks: The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) informed us from Abu al-Qasim Ja'far ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Hammad ibn Isa from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

We asked them (peace be upon them) about a man who fell ill and did not fast until another Ramadan arrived. They said: If he recovered and then delayed (paying the makeup) until another Ramadan arrived, he should fast the days he missed and give charity for each day with a mud of food to a poor person, and he must also pay the makeup. If he remained ill until another Ramadan arrived, he should fast the days he missed and give charity for the first (missed days), one mud for each day to a poor person, and he does not have to pay the makeup.

key_terms.أَدْرَكَهُ: To overtake or arrive upon (referring to the arrival of the next Ramadan).
key_terms.تَوَانٍ: Delay or procrastination in performing an obligation after becoming capable.
key_terms.فِدْيَةٌ: Compensation (charity) given for missing fasts due to valid excuses.
key_terms.قَضَاءُ: Makeup of missed obligatory acts, specifically fasting in this context.
key_terms.مُدّ: A traditional unit of volume for measuring food, used here for the charity payment (fidya).

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for someone who misses Ramadan fasts due to illness and does not make them up before the next Ramadan?
ai.summary: This ruling from al-Isfabar highlights the Shia jurisprudential distinction between temporary and chronic illness, emphasizing that prolonged incapacity exempts one from future makeup fasting (qada) while still requiring compensation (fidya). The requirement of one mud of food per day aligns with the Quranic standard for fidya, reflecting the principle that divine ease is granted according to the duration of the hardship. This specific differentiation underscores the Shia emphasis on precise conditions for religious obligations.
